tool.name: Svelte
tool.tagline: Compiler-based UI framework with fine-grained reactivity through runes
tool.description: Svelte is a UI framework that compiles components into small, fast JavaScript that updates the DOM directly, without a virtual DOM. Svelte 5 expresses reactivity with runes such as $state, $derived and $effect, which work in components and in plain .svelte.js modules. It is used for interactive widgets and full apps, usually together with SvelteKit for routing and server rendering.

glossary.def: A reusable piece of a user interface, such as a button, a card or a whole page. In Svelte each one lives in its own .svelte file with its logic, markup and styles together.
The HTML-like part of a component that describes what appears on screen, with JavaScript values in {curly braces}.
A fast build tool and development server for web projects. In a Svelte project it runs the Svelte compiler on your files and serves the result to the browser.
Processing your code with tools before it's published or run, for example turning .svelte files into plain JavaScript.
Svelte's official app framework. It adds pages and URLs (routing), data loading, building pages on the server, and packaging the app to run somewhere.
An in-memory copy of the page that some frameworks, like React, rebuild and compare on every change to find what to update. Svelte doesn't use one.
CSS in a component's <style> block that Svelte limits to that component's own elements, so it can't affect the rest of the page.
To create a component and insert its elements into the page. Unmounting removes them again.
A special keyword starting with $, such as $state or $derived, that the Svelte compiler recognises and turns into reactive code.
Code or a screen updating itself automatically when the data it depends on changes.
A JavaScript object that wraps another object and is told about every read and change to it. Svelte uses proxies to notice when state objects and arrays change.
A value Svelte computes from other state with $derived, recomputed when that state changes.
In Svelte, a piece of state that a derived value or effect read, so it reruns when that state changes. (Elsewhere the word means a package your project needs.)
In Svelte, a function given to $effect: it runs after the screen updates, and again whenever the state it read changes. Used for side effects such as timers or drawing.
A function that an effect or attachment returns. Svelte calls it before running again and when the component is removed, to stop timers and remove listeners.
A piece of Svelte markup such as {#if}, {#each} or {#await} that shows, repeats or waits for content.
An {#each} block with a key in parentheses, like (todo.id), so Svelte tracks each item by its identity rather than its position.
A two-way link made with bind:, such as bind:value, so an input and a state variable always hold the same value.
A value a parent component passes into a child component, written like an attribute on an HTML tag.
A function passed to a child component as a prop, which the child calls to tell the parent something happened.
A prop the child marks with $bindable(), so a parent can bind: to it and changes made by the child flow back to the parent.
A reusable piece of markup with parameters, declared with {#snippet} and shown with {@render}.
A CSS value with a name starting with --, like --accent, set in one place and read elsewhere with var(--accent).
In Svelte, values a parent component makes available to every component below it, without passing props through each level.
An animation that plays when an element is added to or removed from the page.
A function attached to an element with {@attach}: it runs when the element appears and can return a function that cleans up when it goes away.
A small reactive box holding a value that remembers who read it and tells them when it changes. Svelte 5's reactivity is built from signals.
A small job JavaScript runs right after the current code finishes, before handling anything else, such as the callbacks of resolved promises.
Making HTML that was built on the server interactive in the browser: Svelte attaches its code to the existing page instead of rebuilding it.
In SvelteKit, a function named load in a route's +page.js or +page.server.js file that fetches the data the page needs before it is shown.
In SvelteKit, a function in +page.server.js that handles an HTML form submitted to the server. It works even without JavaScript in the browser.
A SvelteKit add-on that packages your app for the place it will run, such as a Node.js server, static file hosting or a cloud platform.
Your own HTML tag, like <my-counter>, defined with JavaScript and usable in any page or framework.
A browser feature that hides an element's insides from the rest of the page, so outside CSS and scripts can't accidentally change them.
Building a page's HTML once, when the app is built, so it can be served as a plain file to every visitor.

concepts.name: Svelte components and files
concepts.summary: Create a project, write a .svelte component with its JavaScript, markup and styles, and put it on the page.
concepts.why: Everything in Svelte is a component file; knowing its three parts is the starting point for all the rest.
concepts.body: Building an interactive page with plain JavaScript means a lot of DOM code by hand: find the element, change its text, add a listener, remember to update it again later. A **framework** is ready-made code that takes that work off your hands. Svelte is a framework for building a **user interface**: what people see and click. In Svelte you split the page into **components**: reusable pieces such as a button, a card or a whole page, each in its own `.svelte` file. Browsers can't read `.svelte` files. Svelte is a **compiler**, a program that translates code into another form before it runs: each component is turned into plain JavaScript that creates and updates the DOM directly. That translation happens in a **build step**, run by **Vite**, a tool that prepares your project's files for the browser and serves them while you develop. Because the work is done in advance, very little extra Svelte code has to run in the browser. Start a project in a terminal with `npx sv create my-app` (`npx` runs a tool without installing it first). It sets up a **SvelteKit** project, Svelte's official app framework that adds pages and URLs. It's recommended even for small apps. A component file has three optional parts: - `
concepts.code: Hello {name.toUpperCase()}!
takeaways: A `.svelte` file = `<script>` + markup with `{expressions}` + scoped `<style>`
Svelte compiles components into plain JavaScript that updates the DOM directly
`npx sv create` sets up a SvelteKit project; `mount()` starts a plain Svelte app
pitfalls: Naming a component in lowercase (`<card />`); it is then treated as an HTML element.

quiz.q: How does Svelte make `<style>` rules apply only to the component's own elements?
options: It doesn't; styles are global by default
It loads a separate copy of the page for every component
The compiler adds a unique hashed class to the component's elements and selectors
It inlines every style as a style attribute
quiz.explain: Svelte scopes CSS while compiling, by adding a generated class like svelte-xyz123 to the component's elements and to its selectors.

concepts.name: Reactive state with $state
concepts.summary: Make variables that update the screen automatically with the $state rune, change them with plain assignments, and change objects and arrays in place.
concepts.why: State that the screen follows automatically is the core of every Svelte component.
concepts.body:
A component's data changes as the user clicks and types, and the screen should follow. Code that updates itself automatically like that is called **reactive**. In Svelte 5 you mark reactive values with **runes**: special keywords starting with `$` that the compiler recognises. The first is **`$state`**:

```js
let count = $state(0);
```

`count` is a normal variable: read it as `count`, update it with `count++` or `count = 5`, and every place in the markup that uses it updates. There are no special methods to call.

When the value is an object or array, `$state` makes it **deeply reactive**: Svelte wraps it in a **proxy**, a stand-in object that is told about every read and change. So changing it in place works too: `todos.push(item)`, `todos[0].done = true` and `user.name = 'Ada'` all update the screen.

Things to know:

- A plain `let x = 0` without the rune is **not** reactive in Svelte 5 components: the screen won't follow reassignments.
- Svelte collects your changes and updates the page once your code has finished, not line by line. If you need the updated page, `await tick()` waits for it.
- Destructuring copies values: `let { name } = user` gives a plain copy that won't update.

- Classes can use runes in their properties: `class Todo { done = $state(false) }`.
- `console.log` of a state object shows the proxy, not your data. Use **`$inspect(value)`** (only active during development) to log the value whenever it changes, or `$state.snapshot(value)` to get a plain copy.

Runes only work in `.svelte` files and `.svelte.js`/`.svelte.ts` modules, and only where a variable or property is declared, not inside arbitrary expressions.
concepts.code:
<script>
  let count = $state(0);
  let todos = $state([
    { text: 'learn runes', done: false },
  ]);
  let plain = 0;                     // NOT reactive

  function add() {
    todos.push({ text: `todo ${todos.length + 1}`, done: false });  // mutation works
  }
  $inspect(todos);                   // logs on every change (dev only)
</script>

<button onclick={() => count++}>clicks: {count}</button>
<button onclick={() => plain++}>plain: {plain}</button>   <!-- stays 0 on screen -->
<button onclick={add}>add todo</button>

{#each todos as todo}
  <label><input type="checkbox" bind:checked={todo.done} /> {todo.text}</label>
{/each}
takeaways: `let x = $state(initial)` makes a reactive variable updated by plain assignment
Objects and arrays in `$state` are deeply reactive proxies; change them directly
Use `$inspect` or `$state.snapshot` to log state, not raw console.log of proxies
pitfalls: Declaring `let count = 0` without `$state` and wondering why the screen never updates.

quiz.q: `let items = $state([]);` and later `items.push('a')`. Does the UI update?
options: Yes, $state arrays are deeply reactive proxies
Only if items is declared with const
No, arrays must be reassigned: items = [...items, 'a']
quiz.explain: Svelte 5 wraps arrays and objects in proxies, so mutating methods like push trigger updates.

concepts.name: Derived values with $derived
concepts.summary: Compute values from other state with $derived and $derived.by; they update automatically and never go out of date.
concepts.why: Derived values keep the screen consistent without duplicating state or copying values around by hand.
concepts.code:
{stats.done} done, {stats.open} open

    {#each visible as t}
  • {t.text}
    • {/each}
takeaways: `$derived(expr)` recomputes when state it reads changes
`$derived.by(() => {...})` for multi-statement logic
Prefer derived over effects that copy state around
pitfalls: Using `$effect` to set one `$state` from another; that is exactly what `$derived` is for.

quiz.q: `let total = $derived(price * qty)`. The user changes qty. When is total recalculated?
options: Only on the next page load
Immediately on every keystroke even if nothing reads it
Lazily, the next time total is read
quiz.explain: Deriveds are marked dirty when a dependency changes and recomputed when something reads them.

concepts.name: Logic blocks: if, each, key
concepts.summary: Show content conditionally with {#if}, repeat markup with keyed {#each}, and recreate content with {#key}.
concepts.why: Conditionals and lists appear on nearly every screen, and keys decide whether list items keep their state.
concepts.body:
Svelte markup uses **logic blocks** to show, repeat or recreate content. They open with `#`, continue with `:` and close with `/`. **Conditionals**: ```svelte {#if user}

Hi {user.name}

{:else if loading}

Loading...

{:else} {/if} ``` **Lists** with `{#each}`: - `{#each items as item}` or `{#each items as item, i}` for the index. - Destructure directly: `{#each users as { id, name }}`. - An `{:else}` branch is shown when the list is empty. - Add a **key** in parentheses: `{#each todos as todo (todo.id)}` — a **keyed each**. With a key, Svelte moves, inserts and removes the matching elements on the page. Without one it updates elements in place by position, so a focused input or a child component's own state can end up on the wrong item after insertions or deletions. Keys are also required for list animations (an Advanced lesson). `{#each}` accepts arrays, array-like objects and other iterables such as Sets (they are converted with `Array.from`). **`{#key value}`** destroys and recreates its content whenever `value` changes. Use it to restart an animation or reset a child component's state when, say, the selected id changes. `{@html markup}` inserts a string as raw HTML. Only use it with content you trust: HTML typed by users could carry harmful code (XSS).
concepts.code:
{#each todos as todo, i (todo.id)} {:else}

Nothing to do!

{/each} {#if todos.every((t) => t.done)}

All done

{:else}

{todos.filter((t) => !t.done).length} left

{/if} {#key selected}

Details for #{selected}

{/key}
takeaways: `{#if}...{:else if}...{:else}...{/if}` for conditionals
`{#each list as item, i (item.id)}` with a stable key; `{:else}` for empty lists
`{#key x}` recreates its content whenever x changes
pitfalls: Leaving out the key in lists whose items are reordered or removed, so per-item state sticks to the wrong item.

quiz.q: What does the `(todo.id)` part of `{#each todos as todo (todo.id)}` do?
options: Gives each item an identity so Svelte can move and remove the right elements
Filters out todos without an id
Sets the id attribute on each element
quiz.explain: It's the key: Svelte matches items between updates by key instead of by position.

concepts.name: Events and bindings
concepts.summary: Handle DOM events with onclick-style attributes, and keep inputs and state matched with bind:value, bind:checked and bind:group.
concepts.why: Interaction and forms are how users change state; bindings remove most repetitive form code.
concepts.body:
In Svelte 5 event handlers are just **attributes** whose names start with `on`: `onclick={handler}`, `oninput={(e) => ...}`, `onsubmit={save}`. If the handler variable has the same name, use the shorthand `{onclick}`.

There are no event modifiers any more (the old `on:click|preventDefault` form is from Svelte 4). Call `e.preventDefault()` yourself, or wrap handlers in a small helper. To handle an event in the capturing phase, on its way down to the element, use `onclickcapture`. Svelte uses **event delegation** for common events like `click` and `input`: one listener at the root dispatches to your handlers, which is efficient but means `e.stopPropagation()` in a manually added listener can interfere.

**Bindings** create two-way links between an element's properties and state with `bind:`:

- `bind:value={name}` on inputs, textareas and selects (`type="number"` and `range` give numbers).
- `bind:checked={agree}` on checkboxes.
- `bind:group={choice}` on a set of radios (single value) or checkboxes (array of values).
- `bind:this={el}` gives you the DOM element (set once it's mounted).
- Read-only size bindings such as `bind:clientWidth={w}`.

The shorthand `bind:value` binds to a variable called `value`. Bindings need a `$state` variable (or a bindable prop, a later lesson) on the other end. For custom conversion, Svelte 5.9+ supports function bindings: `bind:value={() => get(), (v) => set(v)}`.
concepts.code:
{#each ['vanilla', 'chocolate'] as f} {/each}

{log.join(', ')}
takeaways: Events are attributes: `onclick={fn}`; call `e.preventDefault()` yourself
`bind:value`, `bind:checked`, `bind:group` keep inputs and state matched
`bind:this` gives the element once mounted
pitfalls: Writing `onclick={doThing()}`, which calls the function while the page is being built; pass `doThing` or `() => doThing()`.

quiz.q: How do you prevent a form's default submission in Svelte 5 runes mode?
options: Call e.preventDefault() inside the onsubmit handler
quiz.explain: Event modifiers were removed from the new event attribute syntax; handlers call preventDefault themselves.

concepts.name: Props with $props
concepts.summary: Pass data into components and read it with $props(), including defaults, renaming and rest props.
concepts.why: Props are how components are configured and composed; every reusable component has them.
concepts.body:
Components receive inputs as **props**. Inside the child, read them with the **`$props`** rune and destructure:

```js
let { title, count = 0, ...rest } = $props();
```

- Default values use normal destructuring defaults (`count = 0`), applied when the parent passes `undefined`.
- Rename with `{ class: klass }`, useful for names JavaScript reserves, like `class`.
- `...rest` collects everything else, handy for forwarding attributes to an element: `<button {...rest}>`.
- With TypeScript, annotate: `let { title, count = 0 }: { title: string; count?: number } = $props();`.

The parent passes props as attributes: `<Counter title="Clicks" count={5} />`, `{title}` shorthand when the variable has the same name, and `{...obj}` to spread an object.

Props are **reactive**: when the parent changes the value, destructured variables update too (the compiler makes this work). They are not meant to be reassigned by the child. You can temporarily reassign a prop locally (it will be overwritten when the parent passes a new value), but mutating an object prop the child doesn't own triggers a dev warning (`ownership_invalid_mutation`). To let a child change parent state, pass a function the child can call, or use a bindable prop (later lessons).

Every prop is optional unless typed otherwise; missing ones are `undefined`. `$props.id()` (5.20+) generates an id unique to this copy of the component, handy for pairing a `<label for>` with an input's `id`.
concepts.code: {label}{#if count > 0} {count}{/if}
takeaways: `let { a, b = default, ...rest } = $props()` reads props
Destructured props stay reactive to parent changes
Don't mutate props you don't own; use callbacks or bindable props
pitfalls: Mutating an object prop in the child to communicate with the parent; it's a dev warning and makes data flow hard to follow.

quiz.q: A parent renders `<Badge count={undefined} />` and Badge declares `let { count = 5 } = $props()`. What is count?
quiz.explain: Destructuring defaults apply when the passed value is undefined.

concepts.name: Side effects with $effect
concepts.summary: Run code after the DOM updates when state changes with $effect, clean up correctly, and know when not to use effects.
concepts.why: Effects connect Svelte state to the outside world: canvases, timers, other people's libraries, localStorage.
concepts.body:
**`$effect(fn)`** runs `fn` after the component is mounted and again whenever state it read changes, after the DOM has been updated. Such a function is an **effect**, and it is for side effects: drawing on a canvas, saving to `localStorage`, setting up a library, sending analytics.

```js
$effect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => elapsed++, interval);
  return () => clearInterval(id);    // teardown
});
```

- **Dependencies are tracked automatically**: any `$state`, `$derived` or prop read while the function runs. Values read after an `await` or inside a `setTimeout` callback are not tracked.
- If the function returns a **teardown** (cleanup) function, it runs before the effect re-runs and when the component is destroyed.
- Effects run only in the browser, never while a page is being built on a server.
- Use `untrack(() => value)` to read something without depending on it.
- `$effect.pre` runs before the DOM update (for example to preserve scroll position).
- Svelte groups changes together, so the effect runs once even if several dependencies changed.

When **not** to use an effect: to compute a value from state (use `$derived`), or to respond to a user action (do it in the event handler). Writing state inside an effect that also reads it can create loops; Svelte throws `effect_update_depth_exceeded` when an effect keeps re-triggering itself.

For one-time setup on mount, an effect that reads no state runs once; `onMount` from `svelte` also still works.
concepts.code: {elapsed} ticks
takeaways: `$effect` runs after mount and after DOM updates when its tracked state changes
Return a teardown function to clean up timers and listeners
Use `$derived` for values and event handlers for user actions; effects are an escape hatch
pitfalls: Reading state after an `await` inside an effect and expecting it to be a dependency.

quiz.q: An effect sets `doubled = count * 2` where doubled is $state. What should you use instead?
quiz.explain: Values computed from other state belong in $derived; it's always in sync and never loops.

concepts.name: Snippets and children
concepts.summary: Pass markup into components with children and named snippets, and render reusable chunks with {#snippet} and {@render}.
concepts.why: Snippets are how Svelte 5 does wrapper components, lists with custom items and reusable pieces of markup.
concepts.body:
A **snippet** is a reusable chunk of markup with parameters, declared with `{#snippet name(params)}...{/snippet}` and rendered with `{@render name(args)}`. Snippets can reference state in the scope where they are declared.

They replace Svelte 4 slots for passing content into components:

- Content placed between a component's tags becomes an implicit **`children`** snippet prop. The child renders it with `{@render children?.()}` (the `?.` handles the case where nothing was passed).
- Snippets declared directly inside a component's tags become props with the snippet's name: write `{#snippet header()}...{/snippet}` inside `<Table>` and the table receives a `header` prop.
- Snippets can take **arguments**, so a child can pass data back, like a list component that renders each row with the parent's snippet: `{@render row(item)}`.

Because snippets are ordinary values you can pass them explicitly (`<List {row} />`), check them (`{#if footer}`), and provide fallbacks with `{:else}` branches.

In TypeScript, type them with `Snippet` from `svelte`: `row: Snippet<[Item]>` (the part in `<...>` lists the snippet's argument types).

Snippets also help within one component: extract a repeated piece of markup into a top-level snippet instead of creating a tiny new component.
concepts.code:
{@render children?.()} {#each items as item (item.id)} {@render row(item)} {:else} {#if empty}{@render empty()}{:else}

No items

{/if} {/each}

Team

{#snippet row(user)}

{user.name} {user.admin ? '(admin)' : ''}

{/snippet}
takeaways: `{#snippet name(args)}` declares markup; `{@render name(x)}` renders it
Content between component tags is the `children` snippet prop
Snippets with parameters let children hand data back to the parent's markup
pitfalls: Forgetting `?.()` when rendering an optional snippet, which throws when the parent passed nothing.

quiz.q: Inside `<Card>...</Card>` the parent writes a paragraph. How does Card render it?
quiz.explain: Svelte 5 passes inner content as the children snippet prop, rendered with @render.

concepts.name: Callback props and $bindable
concepts.summary: Let children notify parents with callback props and create two-way bindable props with $bindable.
concepts.why: Components need to report what happened (selection, submit, close) without coupling to their parents.
concepts.body:
In Svelte 5 a child communicates upward by calling **callback props**, plain functions passed by the parent. There is no special event system: name them like events (`onselect`, `onclose`) and call them:

```js
let { onselect } = $props();
// later
onselect?.(item);
```

The parent passes `<Picker onselect={(item) => (chosen = item)} />`. Callbacks can take any arguments and return values, and TypeScript types them like any function prop. (Svelte 4's `createEventDispatcher` and `on:event` are outdated and slated for removal.)

For form-like components, a **bindable prop** gives two-way binding. The child marks the prop with `$bindable()`:

```js
let { value = $bindable('') } = $props();
```

The parent then may write `<TextInput bind:value={query} />`, and assignments to `value` in the child flow back to `query`. Without `bind:`, the prop behaves like a normal one-way prop. The argument to `$bindable()` is the fallback when the parent passes nothing.

Use bindable props sparingly: they are great for input-like components (text inputs, toggles, sliders) but make data flow harder to trace elsewhere. For most interactions, an explicit callback is clearer.

Forwarding is easy: since handlers are props, `...rest` spread on an element passes `onclick` and friends through to the DOM.
concepts.code:
history.push(v ? 'enabled' : 'disabled')} />

dark = {dark}; {history.join(', ')}
takeaways: Children call callback props (`onselect?.(x)`) to notify parents
`let { value = $bindable() } = $props()` allows `bind:value` from the parent
Prefer callbacks; reserve bindable props for input-like components
pitfalls: Using `bind:` on a prop that wasn't declared with `$bindable()`; Svelte reports an error.

quiz.q: A child declares `let { open = $bindable(false) } = $props()`. The parent writes `<Dialog open={show} />` (no bind:). The child sets open = true. What happens to show?
options: show is unchanged; without bind: the prop is one-way
quiz.explain: Bindable props only flow back when the parent uses bind:; otherwise the child changes its local value.

concepts.name: Styling: scoped CSS, class and style
concepts.summary: Style components with scoped CSS, :global, class objects and arrays, class: and style: directives, and CSS custom properties.
concepts.why: Styling is half of UI work, and Svelte's scoping rules decide which selectors actually apply.
concepts.body:
Styles in a component's `<style>` block are **scoped**: Svelte adds a unique generated class to the elements in this component and to your selectors. Consequences:

- Selectors only match elements written in this component's markup, not elements rendered by child components or inserted with `{@html}`.
- Unused selectors produce a compiler warning and are removed.
- Escape scoping with **`:global(...)`**, e.g. `.card :global(p)` to style paragraphs inside children, or a `:global { ... }` block.

For dynamic classes, the **`class` attribute accepts objects and arrays** (Svelte 5.16+, using clsx rules): `class={['btn', { active, disabled: !enabled }, size]}`. Truthy object keys are added, falsy values are skipped. The older **`class:name={cond}`** directive still works, with shorthand `class:active`.

**`style:prop={value}`** sets one inline style property: `style:color={color}`, `style:--progress="{pct}%"`; add `|important` if needed.

To let parents theme a child without breaking scoping, use **CSS custom properties** (named values like `--accent`). The child uses `var(--accent, tomato)`; the parent passes `<Slider --accent="purple" />`, which Svelte applies on a wrapper element.

You can still use Tailwind, CSS modules or global stylesheets; scoped styles are simply the default for component-specific CSS.
concepts.code:
{@html '

from html

'}
takeaways: Component CSS is scoped; `:global(...)` opts out for specific selectors
`class={[..., { name: cond }]}` handles conditional classes; `class:` still works
`style:prop` and CSS custom properties pass dynamic values and theming
pitfalls: Styling a child component's elements from the parent with plain selectors; scoping prevents it, use :global or custom properties.

quiz.q: A parent's `
options: No, the scoped selector only matches elements in the parent's own markup
Only if the child has no style block
quiz.explain: Scoping adds the parent's hash class to the selector, which elements created by the child don't have.

concepts.name: Async data and {#await}
concepts.summary: Load data in components, show loading and error states with {#await}, and avoid showing results that arrive out of order.
concepts.why: Most components show data from a server; the await block handles its three states right in the markup.
concepts.body:
The **`{#await}`** block renders a promise's three states: ```svelte {#await promise}

Loading...

{:then user}

{user.name}

{:catch error}

Failed: {error.message}

{/await} ``` Short forms exist: `{#await promise then value}` skips the loading branch, and `{:catch}` can be omitted. A common approach stores the promise in state, or derives it from other state, so it reloads automatically: ```js let id = $state(1); let userPromise = $derived(fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then((r) => r.json())); ``` When `id` changes a new promise is created and the block shows the pending branch again. The block only renders the result of the **latest** promise, so a slow older response can't overwrite a newer one. Keep in mind: - `fetch` only rejects on network errors; check `res.ok` and throw for HTTP errors so `{:catch}` runs. - When a page is first built on a server (as SvelteKit does), only the pending branch is shown for unfinished promises. In SvelteKit, load data in `load` functions instead (an Advanced lesson), so pages arrive with their data. - For requests that change data (like a POST), call `fetch` in event handlers, not in derived values. Svelte 5.36+ also has an **experimental** mode allowing `await` directly in markup and deriveds, covered in the expert lessons.
concepts.code:
{#await user}

Loading user {id}...

{:then u}

{u.name}

{u.email}

{:catch err}

Could not load: {err.message}

{/await}
takeaways: `{#await p}...{:then v}...{:catch e}{/await}` handles loading, success and error
Derive the promise from state to refetch when inputs change
Throw on non-OK responses so the catch branch runs
pitfalls: Assuming fetch rejects on HTTP 404/500; it resolves, so check `res.ok`.

quiz.q: The user clicks next quickly twice; the first request is slow and resolves last. What does {#await} show?
options: The latest user; results of superseded promises are ignored
quiz.explain: The await block tracks the current promise and ignores results from promises it no longer renders.

concepts.name: Shared state and context
concepts.summary: Share reactive state across components with .svelte.js modules, classes with runes, and context.
concepts.why: Apps need state that many components read: the logged-in user, a shopping cart, a theme. Svelte 5 needs no separate library for it.
takeaways: Runes in `.svelte.js` modules create shared reactive state; export objects, not reassigned variables
Classes with `$state` fields bundle state and methods
Use context (`setContext`/`getContext` or `createContext`) for per-tree and SSR-safe state
pitfalls: Keeping per-user data in module-level state in an SSR app, leaking it between requests.

quiz.q: Why can't you `export let count = $state(0)` from a module and reassign it with count++ elsewhere?
options: Importers get the variable's value, not a live reactive binding, once it is reassigned
quiz.explain: Reassigned exported state can't be tracked across modules; export an object and mutate its properties or use functions.

concepts.name: Transitions and animations
concepts.summary: Animate elements entering and leaving with transition:, in: and out:, animate keyed lists with animate:flip, and tween values.
concepts.why: Built-in motion makes a user interface feel polished with a single attribute instead of an animation library.
concepts.body:
Svelte has motion built in.

**Transitions** play when an element enters or leaves the DOM because of a block (`{#if}`, `{#each}`, `{#key}`):

- `transition:fade` plays both ways; `in:fly={{ y: 20 }}` and `out:fade` set them separately.
- Built-ins in `svelte/transition`: `fade`, `fly`, `slide`, `scale`, `blur`, `draw` (SVG paths) and `crossfade` (send/receive pairs that move an element between lists).
- Parameters such as `duration`, `delay` and `easing` (from `svelte/easing`) are passed as an object.
- Transitions are **local** by default: they run only when their own block changes, not when a parent block is created or destroyed. Add `|global` to change that.
- Events `onintrostart`, `onoutroend` etc. let you react to them.
- Most built-in transitions are implemented with CSS animations, so they stay smooth even while JavaScript is busy.

**`animate:flip`** (from `svelte/animate`) smoothly moves items in a **keyed** `{#each}` when they reorder.

**Motion values**: `Tween` and `Spring` classes from `svelte/motion` (5.8+) animate a number or object over time; set `.target` and read `.current` in markup, for animated counters, progress bars and charts.

Respect users' reduced-motion settings; `prefersReducedMotion` from `svelte/motion` is a reactive boolean to check.

Custom transitions are functions returning `{ duration, css: (t, u) => '...' }` or a `tick` callback.
concepts.code:
{#if show}

Hello!

{/if} {#each items as n (n)}
{n}
{/each}
takeaways: `transition:`, `in:`, `out:` animate elements added or removed by blocks
Transitions are local by default; add `|global` to play with parent blocks
`animate:flip` needs a keyed each; `Tween`/`Spring` animate values
pitfalls: Expecting `animate:flip` to work on an unkeyed `{#each}`; it requires a key.

quiz.q:
A `

` is inside an `{#if a}` which is inside `{#if b}`. b becomes false. Does the fade play?
options: No, transitions are local and only run when their own block changes, unless |global is used
Only if a is also false
quiz.explain: Since Svelte 4 transitions are local by default; destroying an outer block removes the element without the transition.

concepts.name: Attachments and actions
concepts.summary: Run reusable element-level code with {@attach} (and legacy use: actions) for tooltips, keeping focus inside dialogs, and DOM libraries.
concepts.why: Integrating DOM libraries and element behaviours cleanly needs a hook that runs when an element is created.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you need code that runs when a particular element is mounted: initialise a tooltip library, auto-focus, observe size or intersection, add a click-outside handler. Svelte 5.29+ provides **attachments**:

```svelte
<div {@attach (node) => { console.log(node); return () => console.log('cleanup'); }}>
```

An attachment is a function that receives the element and may return a cleanup function. Key properties:

- It runs inside an **effect**: if it reads reactive state, it is torn down and re-run when that state changes. Use a factory that takes arguments: `{@attach tooltip(text)}`, where `tooltip(text)` returns the attachment.
- Attachments can be placed on **components** too: they are passed as props (with a symbol key) and spread onto the element the component forwards `...rest` to. This makes wrapper components transparent.
- Multiple attachments per element are fine; they can be conditional (`{@attach enabled && fn}`).

Before attachments, the same job was done by **actions**: `use:action={param}` with a function `(node, param) => ({ update, destroy })`. Actions still work and many libraries ship them; `fromAction` from `svelte/attachments` converts one into an attachment.

Choose attachments for new code because they compose with props and re-run automatically. Keep heavy work out of them, and always clean up listeners and library instances.
concepts.code:
{#if open}
Menu
{/if}
takeaways: `{@attach fn}` runs fn(element) on mount; a returned function cleans up
Attachments re-run when reactive state they read changes
Actions (`use:`) are the older equivalent; `fromAction` bridges them
pitfalls: Creating listeners or library instances in an attachment without returning a cleanup function.

quiz.q: An attachment created by `tooltip(text)` reads `text`, which is $state. What happens when text changes?
options: The attachment's cleanup runs and the attachment runs again with the new text
Only the DOM text node updates
quiz.explain: Attachments run in an effect, so a change in tracked state tears down and re-runs them.

concepts.name: Reactivity utilities and fine control
concepts.summary: Use $state.raw, $state.snapshot, untrack, reactive Map/Set/URL classes and createSubscriber for precise, efficient reactivity.
concepts.why: Large data, external libraries and custom reactive sources need more control than plain $state.
concepts.body:
Deep proxies are convenient but not free. Svelte gives you finer tools.

- **`$state.raw(value)`** stores the value without proxying. Only reassignment is reactive (`list = [...list, x]`); mutations are ignored. Use it for large arrays or server responses you replace as a whole, and for objects from libraries.
- **`$state.snapshot(value)`** returns a plain, non-proxied deep copy: pass it to `structuredClone`, `JSON.stringify`, charting libraries or anything that dislikes Proxies.
- **`untrack(fn)`** from `svelte` reads state inside an effect or derived without making it a dependency.
- **`svelte/reactivity`** provides reactive versions of built-ins: `SvelteMap`, `SvelteSet`, `SvelteDate`, `SvelteURL`, `SvelteURLSearchParams`. A plain `Map` in `$state` is not made reactive, because only plain objects and arrays are proxied.
- **`MediaQuery`** from the same module is a reactive media query (`new MediaQuery('(min-width: 800px)').current`).
- **`createSubscriber(start)`** turns any external event source into something reactive: reading it inside an effect subscribes, and the source is started and stopped automatically as readers come and go. It is how `MediaQuery` is built.

Equality matters too: setting `$state` to the same primitive value doesn't trigger updates, and `$derived` only notifies when its result changes. Class instances (other than those using runes in fields) are not proxied, so declare reactive properties on the class itself.
concepts.code: {rows.length} rows, {wide.current ? 'wide' : 'narrow'}, visible: {visible.current}
takeaways: `$state.raw` skips proxying: reassign to update
`$state.snapshot` gives a plain copy for libraries and serialisation
Use `SvelteMap`/`SvelteSet`/`SvelteURL` for reactive built-ins; `untrack` to avoid dependencies
`createSubscriber` adapts external event sources
pitfalls: Putting a `Map` in `$state` and calling `.set()`, expecting updates; use `SvelteMap`.

quiz.q: `let data = $state.raw({ n: 1 }); data.n = 2;` Does the UI showing data.n update?
options: No, raw state only reacts to reassignment like data = { n: 2 }
quiz.explain: Raw state is not proxied, so property mutation is invisible to Svelte.

concepts.name: SvelteKit essentials
concepts.summary: Build a full app with SvelteKit: file-based routes, layouts, load functions, form actions and adapters.
concepts.why: Real Svelte apps are usually SvelteKit apps; it adds routing (matching URLs to pages), rendering on the server and data loading.
concepts.body:
**SvelteKit** is the application framework for Svelte, built on Vite. Routes are folders in `src/routes`:

- `+page.svelte` renders a page; `src/routes/blog/[slug]/+page.svelte` handles `/blog/anything`.
- `+layout.svelte` wraps child routes; it renders them with `{@render children()}`.
- `+page.js` or `+page.server.js` exports a **`load`** function that returns data for the page. The page receives it as `let { data } = $props()`. `+page.server.js` runs only on the server, so it can use secret keys and the database; `+page.js` runs on the server for the first request and in the browser when the user moves between pages afterwards.
- `+server.js` exports `GET`, `POST` and other handlers that answer requests for data (endpoints).
- `+error.svelte` renders errors thrown with `error(404, 'Not found')`.

**Form actions** in `+page.server.js` handle `<form method="POST">` submissions on the server; they work without JavaScript, and `use:enhance` from `$app/forms` upgrades them to fetch-based submissions.

Pages are built on the server by default and then **hydrated**: the browser attaches Svelte's code to that HTML to make it interactive. After that, moving between pages happens in the browser without full reloads. Per route you can set `export const prerender = true` to build a page once ahead of time or `ssr = false` for client-only pages.

**Adapters** produce output for a target: `adapter-node`, `adapter-static`, `adapter-vercel`, `adapter-cloudflare` and more. `adapter-auto` detects common platforms.
takeaways: Routes are folders with `+page.svelte`, `+layout.svelte`, `+server.js`
`load` in `+page(.server).js` provides `data`; `.server` files never reach the browser
Form actions handle POSTs and work without JavaScript; `use:enhance` upgrades them
Adapters target Node, static hosting or serverless platforms
pitfalls: Importing database code into `+page.js` (universal) instead of `+page.server.js`, exposing it to the browser bundle.

quiz.q: Where should a load function that queries the database with a secret key live?
quiz.explain: Only .server files are guaranteed to run on the server and are never bundled for the client.

concepts.name: Compiler output and signals
concepts.summary: Understand what the Svelte 5 compiler generates: copied HTML templates, signal-based state, effects and the scheduler that groups updates.
concepts.why: Knowing the runtime model explains performance characteristics and the subtle rules of runes.
concepts.body:
Svelte 5 combines a **compiler** with a small **signal runtime**.

The compiler turns markup into code that creates DOM by cloning a parsed `<template>` element once per component type, then grabs references to the dynamic nodes. Each dynamic part (a text node, an attribute, a block) gets its own small **effect** that updates exactly that node. There is no virtual DOM and no component-level re-render: when `count` changes, only the effects that read `count` run.

Runes compile to signal operations. `let count = $state(0)` becomes a **source signal** (a small box holding the value that remembers who read it); reads become `$.get(count)` and writes `$.set(count, v)`, which is why runes look like plain variables but behave reactively, and why the rules about exports and destructuring exist: the compiler can only rewrite accesses it can see. Proxies created for objects and arrays hold one signal per property, created lazily.

`$derived` is a lazy computed signal; `$effect` and template updates are effects. Svelte uses a **push-pull** model: a write marks dependents dirty (push), and deriveds recompute only when read (pull). Effects are **scheduled** and run together in a **microtask** (a job JavaScript runs right after the current code finishes), so multiple writes cause one update. `flushSync()` forces the updates to run immediately; `tick()` awaits the next one.

Dependencies are collected dynamically on every run, so only state read on the current branch is tracked. You can view the generated JavaScript in the playground's JS output tab.
takeaways: Markup compiles to cloned DOM templates plus one small effect per dynamic part
Runes compile to signal reads and writes (`$.get`, `$.set`)
Push-pull: writes mark dirty, deriveds recompute on read, effects flush in a batch
pitfalls: Assuming a component function re-runs on state change like React; in Svelte only the affected effects run.

quiz.q: When `count` changes in a large Svelte 5 component, what re-executes?
options: A virtual DOM diff of the component
Only the effects (DOM updates, deriveds, $effects) that read count
quiz.explain: Svelte's signals let it update exactly the nodes that depend on the changed state.

quiz.q: Why can't the compiler keep a reassigned `export let x = $state(0)` reactive across modules?
options: Other modules see a plain value; the compiler can only rewrite reads to $.get where it can see the declaration
Exports are copied on every read
quiz.explain: Reactivity of runes depends on compile-time rewriting of accesses, which doesn't happen in importing modules for a reassigned binding.

concepts.name: SSR, hydration, boundaries and async
concepts.summary: Render on the server with svelte/server, hydrate safely, catch errors with svelte:boundary and use experimental await in components.
concepts.why: Building pages on the server and async UI have the trickiest edge cases: mismatches, leaked state and loading coordination.
concepts.body:
**Server-side rendering** (SSR) builds a page's HTML on the server: `render(App, { props })` from `svelte/server` returns `{ head, body }` HTML. Only component scripts and markup run; `$effect`, `onMount` and attachments do not, so browser-only work belongs there. On the client, **`hydrate(App, { target, props })`** adopts the existing DOM instead of recreating it. SvelteKit does both for you.

Hydration expects the client's first render to produce the same output. Non-deterministic values (random ids, `Date.now()`, `window` checks during render) cause mismatches; use `$props.id()` for ids and compute browser-only values in effects. Remember that module-level state is shared across all server requests.

**`<svelte:boundary>`** (5.3+) catches errors thrown while rendering or in effects of its children: provide a `failed` snippet, which receives `(error, reset)`, and an `onerror` callback for logging. This keeps one broken widget from blanking the page.

**Experimental async** (5.36+): with the `experimental.async` compiler option you can `await` directly in `<script>`, in `$derived` expressions and in markup. A boundary's `pending` snippet shows while its contents first load; later updates keep the old UI until new data is ready, and `$effect.pending()` reports in-flight work. Independent awaits in the same markup run at the same time, and updates are coordinated so the UI never shows a mix of old and new data. Because this feature can still change, check the docs before relying on it in a live app.
concepts.code:
{#if $effect.pending()}updating...{/if} console.error(e)}>

{(await getUser(id)).name}

{#snippet pending()}

Loading...

{/snippet} {#snippet failed(error, reset)}

Error: {error.message}

{/snippet}
takeaways: `render` (server) and `hydrate` (client); effects never run on the server
Avoid non-deterministic render output; use `$props.id()` for ids
`<svelte:boundary>` with `failed` and `pending` snippets isolates errors and loading
`await` in markup and deriveds is experimental behind `experimental.async`
pitfalls: Reading `window` or `localStorage` at the top level of a component script, which crashes during SSR.

quiz.q: What does a `failed` snippet on `<svelte:boundary>` receive?
options: The error and a reset function to retry rendering
quiz.explain: The failed snippet is called with (error, reset) so the UI can show the error and retry.

concepts.name: Component API and custom elements
concepts.summary: Mount, unmount and update components from plain JavaScript, compile Svelte components to custom elements, and work with Svelte 4 code.
concepts.why: Using Svelte inside other apps, shipping web components and migrating old code all depend on the low-level component API.
concepts.body:
In Svelte 5 a component is a plain **function**, not a class. You drive it with functions from `svelte`:

- `mount(Component, { target, props })` creates and inserts it, returning its exports; `hydrate` does the same over server-rendered HTML.
- `unmount(instance, { outro: true })` removes it, optionally playing outro transitions (returns a promise).
- Effects created by `mount` don't run immediately; call `flushSync()` when you need the DOM updated immediately, for example in tests.
- To change props from outside, pass a `$state` object as `props` and mutate it; the component sees the changes.
- Components can expose functions or values with `export function` in the script; they appear on the object `mount` returns.

**Custom elements**: with `<svelte:options customElement="my-counter" />` and the `customElement: true` compiler option, a component compiles to a **custom element** (web component): your own HTML tag, usable from any framework or plain HTML. Props become attributes and properties (configure types and reflection with the `props` option), styles are kept inside the element with **shadow DOM** (a browser feature that hides an element's insides from the page's CSS), and `$host()` gives access to the custom element itself, e.g. to dispatch DOM events. Caveats: the inner component is created a tick after the element is connected, passed-in content uses native `<slot>` elements rather than snippets, and context does not cross element boundaries.

**Legacy interop**: Svelte 5 still compiles Svelte 4 syntax (`export let`, `$:`, `on:click`, slots) per component in legacy mode, so you can migrate gradually; `npx sv migrate svelte-5` automates most of it. Runes mode is enabled per file as soon as you use a rune.
takeaways: Components are functions: `mount`, `hydrate`, `unmount`, `flushSync` drive them
Pass a `$state` object as props to update a mounted component from outside
`customElement` compiles to web components; `$host()` reaches the host element
Svelte 4 syntax still compiles per component, so migration can be gradual
pitfalls: Using `new Component({ target })` from Svelte 4; in Svelte 5 use `mount()`.

quiz.q: After `mount(App, { target })` in a test, the DOM is still empty when you assert. Why, and what fixes it?
options: Effects are scheduled, not run synchronously; call flushSync() before asserting
Components only render after a click
quiz.explain: mount schedules effects in a batch; flushSync forces them to run immediately.
